I made a comment here regarding an idea to just block users you are tired of hearing from: https://voat.co/v/AskVoat/comments/86817/148866

I thought about how difficult this might actually be to implement - maybe not exactly difficult to implement in a simple way but I could see how it might be a great strain on the server having to process queries with a long list of not(User A, User B, etc.)

So, what about a client side solution? What I have in mind seems like a simple solution and it's probably a tad naive but...

Simple outline:

  1. User logs in
  2. User chooses other users to block and these settings are saved to their user account.
  3. Blocking settings are transferred from the server and stored in the browser (see http://www.html5rocks.com/en/features/storage))
  4. Use JavaScript and CSS to hide posts and comments from blocked users
  5. Profit?

I've thought before about writing a plugin/bookmarklet to do this on a similar site (cough reddit). It wouldn't take much front end work and the back end seems relatively straightforward.

I honestly wish that they would start to realise the potential value in making Wine more user friendly. Perhaps with a GUI and more initial options then 'please wait while the default wineprefix is being created.'

We do have Winetricks (which hasn't changed one little bit since I first used it YEARS ago) but even that is not ideal. To me, an easy to use, easy to set up Wine could bring in multitudes of new users to Linux who are stuck on Windows but sick of it. Unfortunately for a new user to Wine, even with Winetricks, it's like learning to use a computer all over again.

Maybe it's true that we all want instant gratification these days which means a challenge once in a while is never a bad thing but sometimes Linux is just too fucking stuck in the 80s for it's own good.

I know that there are 3rd party apps for Wine, like PlayOnLinux (which refuses to work with archives, only installers, which renders 90% of my stuff useless with it) and the Codemasters (or Codeweavers?) app which I cannot afford to pay for. But at the very least Wine could provide us with a simple app to choose settings such as the default wineprefix, default install location, all of that before it even goes ahead and creates the default wine folder. I'm sure it isn't out of the realm of possibility to even be able to manage multiple prefixes from the same place.

I feel like it's reached the point of being able to run 90% of windows software and unless they release it with a GUI or claim full support to run absolutely anything, most of these 'updates' are completely pointless to the end user. It still looks the same, still works the same, all the 3rd party tools are still all exactly the same as it all was when I first ever used it years ago. And even then I could already run most of my Windows software problem free. So what's new?

In time, Linux will become more user friendly. There are a lot of alternative applications to use rather than emulating via wine. Updates like this are pointless to the casual end-user, yes. Personally, I use wine to host game servers I couldn't otherwise run on my Ubuntu dedicated server. With some Googling and manual reading, nothing is too difficult to install or get working. My hope is that someday most, if not all developers will think of developing a native Linux app along with OSX and Windows so we can depend on Wine less and less.

I agree with you that it's easy with a bit of Googling, apologies that my comment came out so much like a mad rant. To me it's just the last infuriating step that Linux distros need to make these days and no one seems to get it completely right. I'm fine with the distros that are for advanced users by design, the beauty of Linux is choice. But then you get something like Ubuntu that's user friendly and simple to the point where if you want to do anything other then listen to mp3s or browse the web, you need to be an advanced user anyway because what's provided by the GUI seems to be insulting even to stupid people. What happened to Ubuntu anyway? I first used it on version 9.10 and it was awesome. User friendly enough to just plug and play but without dumbing things down to cellphone level. Now it honestly stinks.

But that is all so off topic. Personally 90% of my Wine use is for games, there aren't many other Windows programs that I miss too much. And that is why for me, and many others, either Windows or Wine will always be necessary. There is a huge library of games that will never be ported to Linux, even if those companies had to become Linux friendly today. And emulating modern Windows to play modern games would require some serious hardware (Wine isn't really an emulator, it's more of a run time or framework). Wine is our best hope. The problem though is that you often spend more time researching and stabbing in the dark to get the game running properly then actually playing it. I would love to see them move forward with the front end as well as the back end, I feel like it's been around long enough now for that.

But of well, there's always dual booting, which I do anyway. How awesome would it be to be able to run two OSs at the same time without rebooting? That would solve a lot of problems.
